hits.text:
claude fable 5.2 is f*cking insane

it can turn 2d blueprints into full 3d walkthroughs that you can tour

these go for $5k to $10k per plan and there's a huge market for them:

> home builders selling homes off plan
> architects presenting a design to a client
> interior designers presenting a renovation
> developers selling apartments off plan
> kitchen and bath remodelers selling upgrades

here's how to start this business:

> pick one niche and find businesses with plans on their site
> give fable the blueprint and their photos
> it renders a few rooms with gpt image 2.5 or a short clip with seedance as the sample
> send them the sample of their own plan before you pitch
> once they pay, fable builds the full walkthrough to scale
> charge per plan to do the rest of their catalog

give this prompt to fable to get started:

<role>
you find businesses that sell spaces from drawings and turn their 2d floor plans into photoreal homes you can walk through in a browser. you handle the outreach and the build. every room is judged against the client's own photos, and nothing ships until it holds up next to them.
</role>

<brief>
- niche: [home builders / architects / interior designers / developers / remodelers]
- area: [state or city]
- offer: a free sample of their own plan, then the full walkthrough per plan
- my details: [name, email, calendar link]
- i'm away and won't answer questions. make the calls yourself and keep going.
</brief>

<find_leads>
- use the apify google maps scraper to pull every [niche] in [area] with a website
- use the apify website content crawler on each site and keep the ones with floor plans or renders on their pages but no walkable 3d tour
- for each one, save the plan drawing and photos of their best plan, the sales or owner contact, and a one line note on how they sell today
- only use public pages and plain requests. never work around bot checks
</find_leads>

<sample>
- before any 3d work, render three rooms from the plan with gpt image 2.5, matched to their photos, or a short walkthrough clip with seedance
- draft a short email with the sample and the offer. no invented prices, numbers or claims
- put business, plan, sample, contact and email in a sheet and show me before anything is sent
</sample>

<build>
once a client pays:
- trace the drawing into one data file of walls, openings and rooms. draw it back over the original and measure the overlap before any 3d work
- build only the main rooms. entry, main living space, kitchen, patio, yard. close the doors on the rest
- build everything in code. blender with python for the shell, furniture and textures. three.js for the viewer. no downloaded models or textures
- bake the light with a film quality renderer so the browser only displays it. direct sun in every interior, picked by measurement not by eye
- fidelity isn't appeal. style each room so it looks photographed and sells
- their listed upgrades as options you can step into inside the room, with a running price and a lead form that records what the buyer explored
- the deliverable is the live page, not a video. host it and make it run on a phone
</build>

<critic_loop>
the builder never grades its own work.
- after each room, send renders and the client's photos to a fresh critic that has seen none of the work
- it answers with a yes or no, at most five problems ranked, each with a fix in numbers, and what is already good
- fix the worst first, render again, send to a new critic. repeat until yes
- for choices of taste, show a critic both versions labelled a and b and let it pick
</critic_loop>

<deliverables>
- the lead sheet with samples and drafted emails, for my approval
- per paid client: the hosted walkthrough link, a contact sheet of every room, the critic log, and a note on anything a human should still check
</deliverables>

THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 at once, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Better results and way fewer tokens, because every task lands on the right model.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and coordinates the work
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5 in its own context
> audit checks the diff on Haiku 5.5 in a throwaway worktree
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reviews the synthesized diff before sign-off
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Reconfigure my Claude Code setup around this tree:
1. Run the main session on Sonnet 5.5 with Opus 5.5 as advisor.
2. Create three Haiku 5.5 subagents in .claude/agents: search (maps the repo), grep (finds call sites), audit (checks the diff).
3. Set isolation: worktree on audit so its checks never touch my working branch.
4. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: delegate every repo search and test run to the Haiku 5.5 subagents to keep the main context small.
5. Route fast deterministic forks (tool choice, path selection, retries) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

↳ https://t.co/YqkjQiqRGv

save it, it'll come in handy.

Stop spending Opus context on grunt work. Anthropic's Claude Code trick splits one session across three models so each does only what it's good at.

Launch it with:
claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

Who does what:
- Sonnet 5.5 drives the session, writes code, applies fixes
- Haiku 5.5 subagents fan out over the repo in parallel to search, grep and audit diffs

WHILE YOU SLEPT, ONE MODEL SPENT 10 DAYS BREAKING LINUX AND FOUND 948 DOORS TO ROOT.

not a hacker group. not a state. a pipeline of OpenAI agents running on $1.2M of API

that kernel runs your server, your Android and the cloud. and it wrote a patch for every door    
           
GPT-6 Cyber is a separate model trained to find bugs and write working exploits. i went through the 27-min report, here's the line stage by stage

▹ what runs under the hood

1. SCOUT agents: 5,034 audit targets · 2.8M lines · 7% of the kernel · $3,426

2. ANALYST agents: 2,308 candidate findings in 12h · $316,549

3. TRIAGE agents: PoC in a KASAN VM, retry until it crashes · 1,724 reproduced in 30h · 74.7% hit rate · only 3.1% wrong analysis

4. EXPLOITDEV agents: SMEP · SMAP · KASLR on, stock distro · 1,169 working root shells · 948 distinct bugs · $1,279 per bug

5. PATCH agents: a patch for every bug · 304 critical sent to maintainers first · humans review before anything ships

6. same harness, new brain: GPT-5.6 Sol in july → 166 · GPT-6 Cyber in october → 948 · 5.7x

SCOUT → ANALYST → TRIAGE → SCREEN → EXPLOITDEV → PATCH → HUMAN

firefox: 81 new high-severity bugs. Mozilla already shipping fixes (MFSA 2026-118). Mozilla and Palo Alto Networks are on Cyber already

cost: $1.2M in API for one run. at Pwn2Own / TyphoonPWN prices those 948 exploits are worth $18.9M–$66.3M

access: no public release. GPT-6 Cyber goes to approved orgs via Daybreak Red, behind an IP allowlist. defenders get GPT-6 Astra via Daybreak Blue. everyone else: plain Astra

▹ the edge

alone each agent is mid. together they're a loop: find → prove → break → fix, and you rerun it on every new model

OpenAI own line: a low-privilege account on an unpatched box = root for a well-funded attacker. bot, hot wallet or validator key on a linux server you haven't updated? that's your threat model now

10 days after the scan: 61 fixes upstream · 43 staging · 299 discussed in public. the patch race already started

will models fix the internet faster than they break it?

virals.text:
In April, Anthropic employees sold $4.66 billion of their stock.

This morning's IPO filing puts those same shares at about $13.3 billion. Selling seven months early cost them roughly $8.6 billion.

And that was the small group that wanted out. Investors showed up ready to buy about $6 billion at $25.91 a share, and employees wouldn't sell enough to fill the order. Today's price range is $70 to $78.

Some of that comes down to who Anthropic hires. Its culture interview asks candidates how they'd feel if a safety decision sent the stock to zero. Screen every recruit for comfort with zero and you end up with a cap table full of people who won't sell at a $350 billion valuation.

The $100M math in this tweet assumed a $2 trillion company. Today's range comes out to $1.26 to $1.41 trillion fully diluted, and about $1 trillion on shares outstanding. So every one of those paper fortunes just shrank by about a third.

"Liquid" is doing a lot of work in there too. On day one, some employees can sell up to 10% of their locked shares. Another 35% opens up after the full-year 2026 results come out. Everything else waits for Q1 2027 earnings or 180 days, whichever hits first. If you're sitting on $100M on paper, you can turn maybe $10M of it into cash the first week, and that's before taxes.

I held options through the ThredUp IPO. The number on your brokerage screen and the number you can actually spend stay two different numbers for a long time.

Also, most of the people at Anthropic today are new. The company had about 940 employees at the end of 2024 and 5,300 by September. More than four out of five joined in the last 21 months, and most of them couldn't have sold in April anyway because the tender required a year of tenure. Meanwhile, over 75 of the first 100 employees are still there, sitting on grants from back when the company was worth a few billion dollars.

Anthropic made its recruits picture the stock going to zero. Kind of funny that the harder test turned out to be holding at $25 a share while investors were waving $6 billion in their faces.

outsiders.text:
THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 at once, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Better results and way fewer tokens, because every task lands on the right model.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and coordinates the work
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5 in its own context
> audit checks the diff on Haiku 5.5 in a throwaway worktree
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reviews the synthesized diff before sign-off
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

2. Create three Haiku 5.5 subagents in .claude/agents: search (maps the repo), grep (finds call sites), audit (checks the diff).
3. Set isolation: worktree on audit so its checks never touch my working branch.
4. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: delegate every repo search and test run to the Haiku 5.5 subagents to keep the main context small.
5. Route fast deterministic forks (tool choice, path selection, retries) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

save it, it'll come in handy.

outsiders.draft_en:
Stop spending Opus context on grunt work. Anthropic's Claude Code trick splits one session across three models so each does only what it's good at.

Launch it with:
claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

- Haiku 5.5 subagents fan out over the repo in parallel to search, grep and audit diffs
- Opus 5.5 sits on call as advisor and signs off on the final diff

outsiders.name: cryptopsihoz
outsiders.text:
WHILE YOU SLEPT, ONE MODEL SPENT 10 DAYS BREAKING LINUX AND FOUND 948 DOORS TO ROOT.

not a hacker group. not a state. a pipeline of OpenAI agents running on $1.2M of API

that kernel runs your server, your Android and the cloud. and it wrote a patch for every door    
           
GPT-6 Cyber is a separate model trained to find bugs and write working exploits. i went through the 27-min report, here's the line stage by stage

▹ what runs under the hood

1. SCOUT agents: 5,034 audit targets · 2.8M lines · 7% of the kernel · $3,426

2. ANALYST agents: 2,308 candidate findings in 12h · $316,549

3. TRIAGE agents: PoC in a KASAN VM, retry until it crashes · 1,724 reproduced in 30h · 74.7% hit rate · only 3.1% wrong analysis

4. EXPLOITDEV agents: SMEP · SMAP · KASLR on, stock distro · 1,169 working root shells · 948 distinct bugs · $1,279 per bug

5. PATCH agents: a patch for every bug · 304 critical sent to maintainers first · humans review before anything ships

6. same harness, new brain: GPT-5.6 Sol in july → 166 · GPT-6 Cyber in october → 948 · 5.7x

SCOUT → ANALYST → TRIAGE → SCREEN → EXPLOITDEV → PATCH → HUMAN

firefox: 81 new high-severity bugs. Mozilla already shipping fixes (MFSA 2026-118). Mozilla and Palo Alto Networks are on Cyber already

cost: $1.2M in API for one run. at Pwn2Own / TyphoonPWN prices those 948 exploits are worth $18.9M–$66.3M

access: no public release. GPT-6 Cyber goes to approved orgs via Daybreak Red, behind an IP allowlist. defenders get GPT-6 Astra via Daybreak Blue. everyone else: plain Astra

▹ the edge

alone each agent is mid. together they're a loop: find → prove → break → fix, and you rerun it on every new model

OpenAI own line: a low-privilege account on an unpatched box = root for a well-funded attacker. bot, hot wallet or validator key on a linux server you haven't updated? that's your threat model now

10 days after the scan: 61 fixes upstream · 43 staging · 299 discussed in public. the patch race already started

will models fix the internet faster than they break it?

outsiders.name: Aakash Gupta
outsiders.text:
In April, Anthropic employees sold $4.66 billion of their stock.

This morning's IPO filing puts those same shares at about $13.3 billion. Selling seven months early cost them roughly $8.6 billion.

And that was the small group that wanted out. Investors showed up ready to buy about $6 billion at $25.91 a share, and employees wouldn't sell enough to fill the order. Today's price range is $70 to $78.

Some of that comes down to who Anthropic hires. Its culture interview asks candidates how they'd feel if a safety decision sent the stock to zero. Screen every recruit for comfort with zero and you end up with a cap table full of people who won't sell at a $350 billion valuation.

The $100M math in this tweet assumed a $2 trillion company. Today's range comes out to $1.26 to $1.41 trillion fully diluted, and about $1 trillion on shares outstanding. So every one of those paper fortunes just shrank by about a third.

"Liquid" is doing a lot of work in there too. On day one, some employees can sell up to 10% of their locked shares. Another 35% opens up after the full-year 2026 results come out. Everything else waits for Q1 2027 earnings or 180 days, whichever hits first. If you're sitting on $100M on paper, you can turn maybe $10M of it into cash the first week, and that's before taxes.

I held options through the ThredUp IPO. The number on your brokerage screen and the number you can actually spend stay two different numbers for a long time.

Also, most of the people at Anthropic today are new. The company had about 940 employees at the end of 2024 and 5,300 by September. More than four out of five joined in the last 21 months, and most of them couldn't have sold in April anyway because the tender required a year of tenure. Meanwhile, over 75 of the first 100 employees are still there, sitting on grants from back when the company was worth a few billion dollars.

Anthropic made its recruits picture the stock going to zero. Kind of funny that the harder test turned out to be holding at $25 a share while investors were waving $6 billion in their faces.
